source.title: How AI agents shape experts’ judgment calls
source.scope: Read the complete Anthropic study covering analyst recruitment, artificial pro and con agent lean, recommendation switching, repeated argument effects, accuracy and time results, authorship attribution, study limitations and the distinction between experimental prompts and workplace use.
source.freshness_reason: No newer lane-matched study with comparable expert-decision evidence survived the bounded search. This October 27 original uses the justified 168-hour fallback, with the limited search scope disclosed separately.

read_evidence.scope: Read the complete Anthropic study covering analyst recruitment, artificial pro and con agent lean, recommendation switching, repeated argument effects, accuracy and time results, authorship attribution, study limitations and the distinction between experimental prompts and workplace use.

coverage_labels: Applied Generative AI for Knowledge Workers
stories.related_coverage: Shows why decision-support agents need independent evidence review and recorded disagreement instead of treating fluent recommendations as neutral analysis.
stories.summary: Anthropic studied analysts using agents that were experimentally steered toward favorable or unfavorable recommendations. Participants often moved toward the agent’s position, repeated its arguments and rarely credited the system, even while completing work faster. The controlled setting and uneven comparison groups limit workplace generalization, so the results identify a review risk rather than a universal effect.
stories.why_it_matters: Analyst teams can add a simple countermeasure: record the initial judgment, inspect primary evidence before the recommendation, require a written disagreement check and preserve attribution. Those controls expose influence without banning useful assistance.
stories.image_alt_intent: An analyst compares an initial judgment with an agent recommendation, primary evidence, a counterargument checklist and a final attributed decision.

fallback_decisions.why_selected_over_recent_options: GDPx was selected over the same-date Momentic QA benchmark because its expert-authored professional deliverables span eleven domains and directly support the technical evaluation lane; Momentic is a narrower browser-testing benchmark. Date-only timestamps do not prove either item was inside the rolling 24-hour window.

The NVIDIA Cosmos article was selected because it documents an implementable interactive world-simulation pipeline with model, sensor and deployment constraints. Same-date Lakebase and Momentic items cover application databases and QA agents, not interactive simulation; date-only timestamps provide no rolling-24-hour proof.

The bounded search found no newer lane-matched original study with comparable evidence about experts changing judgment after agent advice. Same-date Lakebase and Momentic items concern application infrastructure and browser testing, so neither displaced the October 27 human-decision study.
